pages.title: India-USA: official status and leaders' views
pages.summary: India and the USA are strategic partners, with a dialogue since 2010 that was later widened into a strategic and commercial dialogue resting on five pillars. The page lists how Vajpayee, Manmohan Singh, Modi, Obama, Ashton Carter and Hillary Clinton described the relationship.

pages.title: Estranged democracies to quasi-alliance: Pant and Mattoo
pages.summary: Mattis and Jeff Davis call ties with India a top priority and pivotal, and the notes recall Dennis Kux's 'estranged democracies' and David Malone's blind-man-and-elephant image. Cold War non-alignment leaned to the Soviet bloc and turned anti-American, which Harsh Pant calls once typical and Amitabh Mattoo calls a thing of the past.

pages.title: Systemic, domestic and personal drivers; wide cooperation
pages.summary: Harsh Pant attributes the change to systemic factors (end of bipolarity, rise of China), economic compulsions and individual leaders, helped by the Indian American lobby and Ashley Tellis's role in de-hyphenation. The page lists trade above 100 billion dollars, FDI, Asia rebalance and Act East convergence, and exercises such as Malabar, Yuddha Abhyas and RIMPAC.

pages.title: Defence cooperation, nuclear support and Trump concerns
pages.summary: Red Flag air exercises, US arms supply, DTTI and major defence partner status are listed alongside US help on the NSG waiver, MTCR entry and a UNSC seat. Trump's Buy American and Hire American policy is flagged as a cause of uncertainty as India builds its own manufacturing sector.

pages.title: America First versus Make in India
pages.summary: George Verghese sees Trump's policy as ideological (anti-Islamic) and transactional (commercial), with commerce likely to decide, and gaps remain on investment, IPR, WTO agriculture and climate change. Lisa Curtis calls the partnership transactional, with India preferring strategic autonomy, and Kanwal Sibal names H1B as the main direct grievance.

pages.title: Indian scholars on India-US ties under Trump
pages.summary: Sibal warns of collateral damage, Rakesh Sood calls it an age of uncertainty, Manoj Joshi says India can offset China, and Nandan Unnikrishnan urges caution on G2. Verghese says India is not Trump's top priority, so the partnership may run on autopilot amid open questions on China and counter-terrorism.

pages.title: Pre-independence views and the 1960s conflict phase
pages.summary: The page closes the Trump section by saying India is too big and proud to play junior partner. It then begins the evolution of ties, noting Nehru's warning about American imperialism and Phase I conflicts such as Kashmir at the UNSC and India recognising communist China.

pages.title: Phase I cooperation; Phase II conflict, 1970s-1990s
pages.summary: Phase I cooperation included US help in 1962, neutrality in 1965 and aid on food security and the Green Revolution, yet India kept anti-American rhetoric and a US-Pakistan-China axis formed. Phase II was pure conflict: the USSR treaty, the India-USSR-Vietnam axis, 1971 threats and US apathy after Pokhran I.

pages.title: Post-Cold War phase and Talbott-Jaswant Singh talks
pages.summary: In 1989 India allowed US refuelling in the Gulf War, and Ashley Tellis ties the partnership to China's rise and the balance of power, though Pokhran II brought sanctions again. The Talbott-Jaswant Singh talks of 1998-2000 met 14 times to push India toward NPT and CTBT.

pages.title: Kargil, Clinton visit, 9/11 and Next Steps
pages.summary: The talks laid the foundation of strategic partnership, and the USA took a pro-India stand in Kargil, followed by Clinton's 2000 visit and a vision statement; 9/11 disappointed India as Pakistan became a frontline state. Vajpayee's 2004 visit launched Next Steps in Strategic Partnership covering civil nuclear, high technology and space, consultation and institutional dialogue.

pages.title: 1-2-3 agreement, plateau and Modi's tilt
pages.summary: The 2005 1-2-3 agreement is called the biggest achievement, with the USA going extra miles for India's civil nuclear integration. Under Obama the partnership plateaued over Doha, climate, the investment treaty, IPR, Afghanistan and Mumbai, while Modi tilts explicitly toward the USA and visited four times in under two and a half years.

pages.title: Modi-Obama initiatives and civil nuclear significance
pages.summary: Modi and Obama released 'chalein sath sath', Obama was Republic Day guest, a joint vision named Asia Pacific, and DTTI, LEMOA, MTCR entry and major defence partner status followed. The civil nuclear agreement is described as geopolitical, integrating India in the non-proliferation regime without NPT or CTBT and recognising it as a de-facto nuclear weapon state.

pages.title: Nuclear deal benefits and India's obligations
pages.summary: Benefits include recognition of India's non-proliferation record and advanced technology, energy security, support for a permanent UNSC seat and use of thorium in the third stage. India's obligations include separating civil and military facilities, IAEA safeguards, the supplementary compensation convention, liability legislation, the testing moratorium and FMCT cooperation.

pages.title: US obligations; why no American reactor arrived
pages.summary: The USA must reform domestic law (Hyde Act), obtain an NSG waiver and India's entry to NSG, MTCR, Australia Group and Wassenaar, and enable full technology transfer. No American reactor has reached India because of US objections to Sections 17(B) and 46, so Russia and France benefited, Westinghouse sought bankruptcy relief and a deal with Japan was needed.

pages.title: Nuclear liability Act: Sections 4, 6 and 17
pages.summary: The page explains supplier no-fault liability (Section 4), the 300 million SDR compensation cap (Section 6) with operator liability of 1500 crore, and operator recourse under Sections 17 to 17(B). The USA objects to 17(B), while India says it follows the convention on supplementary compensation.

pages.title: Section 17(C), insurance pool and Section 46
pages.summary: Modi's answers were that 17(B) makes little difference because contracts state liability, plus an insurance pool led by GIC with a 750 crore government fund. Section 46 allows other liabilities under Indian law, drawing more US objection, and the government says it does not apply to suppliers.

pages.title: Section 46 outcome and Bilateral Investment Treaty gap
pages.summary: Parliament rejected an amendment naming suppliers, but the Supreme Court will decide whether Section 46 applies to them. On the investment treaty, India's 2015 model is enterprise-based and the US 2012 model is asset-based, and India's model has no MFN status.

pages.title: Investment disputes, IPR and patent evergreening
pages.summary: The page covers National Treatment, US wishes on retrospective taxation and international arbitration, and India's steps on arbitration law and dispute redressal. It then opens the IPR dispute, saying the partnership is hijacked by pharmaceutical companies, and explains Section 3 on evergreening.

pages.title: Section 84 compulsory licensing and totalisation
pages.summary: Section 84 allows compulsory licences after three years for public health, high price or non-working, and Bayer lost to NATCO over Nexaver and generic Soranib. Indian professionals pay about 28 billion dollars into US Social Security without benefit, and India wants a totalisation agreement.

pages.title: USTR report, IPR watch lists and defence framework
pages.summary: The 2017 USTR report calls Indian policies harmful and recommends pressure on IPR, cotton and textile subsidies and anti-dumping duties, and India sits on the priority watch list. Defence is called the brightest spot, with the 1995 framework reviewed in 2015 and India the second largest destination for US defence exports after Saudi Arabia.

pages.title: Defence purchases, DTTI, LEMOA and exercises
pages.summary: India has bought Apache and Chinook helicopters, C-17 and C-130 aircraft and P-8 Poseidon aircraft, and is a major defence partner. DTTI makes the two co-producers, and regular exercises and LEMOA build interoperability, a strength the notes contrast with India-Russia ties.

pages.title: Foundational agreements and geopolitical concerns
pages.summary: EUMA and LEMOA are signed, while CISMOA and BECA are pending, with India reluctant over US closeness to Pakistan. The page ends with geopolitical concerns: US ties with Pakistan and China, Afghanistan, the war on terror, the Middle East and Asia Pacific.

flashcards.front: What are the five pillars of the India-USA strategic partnership, and how did the 2010 dialogue change?
flashcards.back: The pillars are strategic issues, energy and climate change, science and technology, health and innovation, and education and development. The institutionalised strategic dialogue begun in 2010 was later changed into a strategic and commercial dialogue.

flashcards.front: Who coined the phrase 'estranged democracies' for India and the USA, and how did David Malone describe their mutual understanding?
flashcards.back: Dennis Kux coined 'estranged democracies'. David Malone described the two as the proverbial blind man and elephant trying to understand each other.

flashcards.front: Which three factors does Harsh B. Pant give for the changed India-US relationship?
flashcards.back: Systemic, domestic and personal factors: the end of bipolarity and rise of China, India's economic compulsions, and the preferences of leaders such as Vajpayee, Modi, Bush and Obama.

flashcards.front: How does Lisa Curtis assess the India-US strategic partnership, and why does India avoid a full alliance?
flashcards.back: She calls it primarily transactional rather than strategic. India prefers multiple alignment and strategic autonomy, has no security doctrine, and focuses mainly on getting defence equipment and technology.

flashcards.front: What was the Strobe Talbott-Jaswant Singh dialogue of 1998-2000, and what did it achieve?
flashcards.back: The US Deputy Secretary of State and the Indian Foreign Minister met 14 times in two years, with the US aiming to push India to give up nuclear weapons and join NPT and CTBT. For the first time the two sides understood each other, which laid the foundation of strategic partnership.

flashcards.front: What obligations did India take on under the India-US civil nuclear agreement?
flashcards.back: India must separate civilian and military nuclear facilities, put civilian ones under IAEA safeguards with an India-specific agreement, and ratify the convention on supplementary compensation. It must also legislate on nuclear liability, continue its testing moratorium and work with the USA for an early FMCT.

flashcards.front: Why does the USA object to Section 17(B) of India's civil nuclear liability Act, and what is India's reply?
flashcards.back: Section 17(B) gives the operator recourse against the supplier for patent or latent defects in materials, equipment and services even if the contract does not say so. The USA says this is not an international norm, while India says it follows the convention on supplementary compensation.

flashcards.front: How do the Indian and American model investment treaties differ?
flashcards.back: India's 2015 model is enterprise-based, requiring substantial physical presence and workforce in India, and it has no MFN status. The US model of 2012 is asset-based, seeking protection for shares, derivatives and intellectual property.

flashcards.front: When can compulsory licensing be granted under Section 84 of the Indian Patents Act, and which case illustrated it?
flashcards.back: It can be granted after three years of a patent for public health, if the medicine is overpriced, or if it is not worked in India. Bayer lost its case against NATCO, whose generic Soranib cost Rs 8,800 against Rs 2,80,000 a month for Nexaver.

flashcards.front: How does the Defence, Trade and Technology Initiative (DTTI) change India-US defence ties?
flashcards.back: DTTI makes India and the USA co-producers rather than just buyers and sellers, starting with pathfinder projects. Together with LEMOA, which makes them at least logistic allies, and regular exercises, it builds interoperability between the armed forces.

answers.question: The India-US strategic partnership has been described as more transactional than strategic. Examine with reference to defence cooperation, economic disputes and the uncertainty of the Trump era.
answers.intro: Once 'estranged democracies', India and the USA are now strategic partners with a strategic and commercial dialogue. Yet Lisa Curtis argues the partnership is primarily transactional, so the label must be tested against defence ties and economic disputes.
body: Transactional core: Lisa Curtis says India avoids becoming an ally, prefers multiple alignment and strategic autonomy, and lacks a security doctrine, so its interest centres on defence equipment and technology.

Defence is the brightest spot: the 1995 framework, DTTI co-production, major defence partner status, LEMOA, EUMA and exercises such as Malabar and Red Flag. CISMOA and BECA stay pending because of US closeness to Pakistan.
Economic friction persists: enterprise-based versus asset-based investment treaty models, IPR disputes over Sections 3 and 84, totalisation, and India's place on the USTR priority watch list.
Trump-era uncertainty: George Verghese sees an ideological and a transactional side, and Buy American clashes with Make in India, while Kanwal Sibal warns of collateral damage.

Strategic logic remains: Ashley Tellis ties US support to balancing China, Rakesh Sood urges agility in an age of uncertainty, and Manoj Joshi says India can offset China's pull if it stays firm on national interest.
answers.conclusion: The partnership is strategic in intent but transactional in practice. Its depth will depend on settling IPR and investment disputes, completing the foundational agreements, and balancing India's strategic autonomy with closer defence integration.

answers.question: The India-US civil nuclear agreement was a strategic breakthrough, yet no American reactor has reached Indian soil. Explain the deal's significance and the role of India's nuclear liability law.
answers.topic: Civil nuclear agreement and liability law
answers.intro: The 2005 agreement integrated India into global civil nuclear commerce without NPT or CTBT membership. It carried geopolitical weight by recognising India as a de-facto nuclear weapon state, but its commercial promise has stalled over liability provisions.
body: Significance: the deal recognises India's non-proliferation record and advanced technology, supports energy security and climate commitments, helps commercialise the thorium-based third stage and strengthens India's claim to a permanent UNSC seat.

Obligations: India separates civil and military facilities, accepts IAEA safeguards, ratifies the supplementary compensation convention and legislates on liability. The USA amends the Hyde Act and seeks an NSG waiver and entry into NSG, MTCR, Australia Group and Wassenaar.

Liability friction: Section 4 imposes no-fault supplier liability, Section 6 caps compensation at 300 million SDR, and Section 17(B) gives operators recourse for latent defects. The USA also objects to Section 46, which keeps other legal liabilities alive.

Modi government's fix: it argued 17(B) changes little because contracts state liability, built a GIC-led insurance pool with a 750 crore government fund, and said Section 46 does not apply to suppliers, though the Supreme Court will decide. Russia and France gained meanwhile, as Westinghouse sought bankruptcy relief.
scholars: Strobe Talbott and Jaswant Singh talks
answers.conclusion: The agreement ended India's nuclear isolation but delivered more strategically than commercially. Clarity from the Supreme Court on Section 46, the insurance pool and wider reactor deals will decide whether the promise of cooperation is met.
